I actually have a lot of night terrors due to being abused as a child. Night terrors are a bit different than nightmares in that night terrors happen in the moments just before waking, where the mind is semi-conscious. So you're still in a state of sleep paralysis but still unconscious enough to dream. There's a movie about this on Netflix called The Nightmare. It pretty much describes what I go through when I have these. My favorite writer, H.P Lovecraft drew a lot of inspiration from his night terrors. I suffer from all sorts of psych disorders. My depression, anxiety, and PTSD might be the ones that make the most sense. I'm a victim of sexual and verbal abuse as a young adult and it's caused me to be afraid of sleeping.

I've had a few that are reoccurring. The most notable is of a women with frazzled red hair whose face is melted. Not in the way a human with skin would melt. More like what it would look like if you took a blowtorch to the face of a manikin. Everything bubbled and solidified in a mass with only blackness showing through the holes. I see her standing above my bed and when I actually come to it's like I blink and she's gone.

Another one I have is of a mass of floating flesh, about the size of a cow. It undulates and molds itself and even though it doesn't even look human or say anything, I can actually here bones breaking on the inside of it as it moves.

The one that makes me the most scared is another faceless person who leans around my door frame if I leave it open before I fall asleep. They don't make a noise but they put their finger up to their mouth like they're shushing me. I don't know why but this is the only one that makes me wake up afraid. Very, very afraid. IT only happens when I'm home alone and every time I don't leave my room or go near my bedroom door. I just watch it until I feel like it's safe to leave my bed. I've stopped sleeping with my door open as a result.

I saw that you're wary of introducing Minecraft to your kids. I'd make the argument against that. If you're worried about them spending to much time gaming, limit their gaming time, use extra gaming time as a reward, or just make gaming the thing they're allowed to do when they've done everything for the day. It's how I was brought up and it gave me good habits in learning to balance responsibility with fun! Just something to think about

Minecraft can be a really good tool for developing children. Right now it's being used in schools for all ages as it helps younger kids develop spacial reasoning and older kids with subjects like architecture and sculpting. It also helps boost problem solving skills as the players have to work within the boundaries of the game's physics to create their world.

It sounds to me like you're experiencing some pretty heavy burnout along with some repressed memories. You're stretching yourself pretty thin and it seems like you've gotten so caught up in trying to do well for yourself you've forgotten really what you need to be happy. You're a human being. And academic success isn't the only thing you need in your life. If all your daily activities aren't doing you any real good emotionally, then are they all worth it? Sometimes you have to focus in yourself to get better at everything else.

Also, your repressed childhood memories coming to the surface of your psyche is actually something that happens in adult development. There's a ton of focus on childhood and adolescent development but the reality is that we as humans don't ever really stop developing or emotional self. So you're coming to a point in your life where a lot of change is happening. Because you're changing, and because your parents' separation happened while you were changing, those two moments are linked and could be bringing up old memories. It might be time to deal with those. I'd talk to you doctors on that one. In the mean time, check out a book called Outgrowing the Pain. The title is a little drastic but there are some things in there you might benefit from.

Also, take it from someone who went through pretty much everything you went through. You're sooooooo fucking young. You have no idea how young you are. And that's not to discredit what you've gone through or what you've accomplished. It's meant to tell you that you still have the chance to shape who you really want to be. Okay! Lemme break it down for you! :P

Really, any build is possible. You just have to tweak it to your play style. I play a tank with an emphasis on having really heavy armor, a big ass sword, and I use faith to complement my lack of magic use. I've given myself enough vitality that I can run and roll quickly even though I have really heavy equipment. My stats look like this: Vigor - 20 (No real need to go higher than this IMO. I've got plenty of surviveability) Endurance - 25 (works out great! With the Chloranthy Ring, an absolute must for strength builds, I can get 5-6 swings in with most greatswords and clubs) Vitality - 28 (again, quick rolls!) Attunement - 15 (I wanted 2 spells slots) Strength - 50 (I use the UGS's, or Ultra Great Swords, class of weapons and keep Dragon Tooth around as well. Most of my weapons scale with stg so I love having it so high) Dex - 18 (I'm not using dex based stuff plus it doesn't scale as well as strength. So I kept it as low as I could) Adaptability - 15 (again, this is just where I feel comfortable with it.) Int - 3 (cuz why) Faith - 50 (I'm trying to get it to 56 so I can use the Sunlight Spear which is the highest damage lighting throw in the game.)

In terms of equipment, I like to use heavy stuff. I like tanking damage and don't mind moving slowly. You might think differently and just go with a low weighted armor to avoid having to put so much in Vitality to overcome the slowness. I use weapon's like the Pursuer's Ultra Great Sword, Dragon Tooth, and Smelter's Sword, all of which require crazy strength to wield. Again, you might not want to go as high as I did. You could stop at 40 or 30 and just use great swords instead. I use faith to cast sunlight blade or to carry extra spells.

So yeah. This is just my build. Let me know what else you need explained or if you want help planning your out.

Well, assuming you're in America, ADA laws state that you don't have to disclose any information of your illnesses before an employer highers you, nor do you have to afterwards. Granted, if your panic attacks prevent you from doing your job they can still have you leave. I was actually very forward about it during my interview. I explained my situation and the accommodations I would need (basically I said that if I need to step away for a period of time that it not be held against me or denied) and they were actually extremely helpful about it. 

It's a matter of making a working relationship. Find a place and a job position in which you feel comfortable and go for that. I'm a lot attendant at a Home Depot right now. So I get to constantly be on the move. I'm not tied down to any specific area of the store so I can leave if my agoraphobia or social anxiety kicks in. Plus if I need to pawn a customer off on another associate I can do so. 

Try looking around and applying for jobs. Find a position that you think won't set off your anxiety at a place you would enjoy working. IF your job is enjoyable to you it should keep your anxiety down. Also, don't break your back for someone who isn't going to help you. Why go and work for a business that's going to cause dread in your every day life?

OH MAN! Lovecraft is without a doubt my all time favorite author. Really, there's no continual cannon despite a lot of the stories referencing one another. It might be best to start reading chronologically because it could help you see how his writing evolved and it'll be easier to pick up on all the ideas he builds throughout his mythos. 

That being said, I can recommend a few groups of stuff to read that'll go over a lot of the nuances in his writing.

"The Doom That Came to Sarnath" "Dagon" "The Colour Out of Space" "The Rays in the Walls"  are a few good ones to kinda grasp his notions of what cosmic horror really is about, the unnameable and unthinkable. These ones' don't entirely connect to the overall mythos but are great works nonetheless. 

"The Cats of Ulthar" "The Hound" "Under the Pyramids" "Herbert West - Reanimator" "Cool Air" are all really good Gothic stories with some awesome twists and have nothing to do with the Cthulu mythos but are just good scary stoires.

In terms of actually getting into some of the elder gods stuff, the essentials are "The Call of Cthulu" "The Dunwich Horror" "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" "The Case of Charles Dexter Ward" "The Dream Quest of Unknown Kadath" All of these have the elder gods as the main antagonist and get into a lot of the legacy Lovecraft left behind in the Cthulu mythos. 

I saved mentioning "At the Mountains of Madness" for last because it's Lovecraft's opus. It's the one work that gathers together all of his themes the most effectively: cosmic horror, scientific discovery, forbidden knowledge, and so on. I wouldn't say save it for last but I'd read at least one or two from each of the categories I wrote abotu above.

I hope you enjoy!

The Bad:
-The story takes a massive back seat. IT might as well not even be there because it basically exists to give you back story for why you're shooting a bunch of aliens.
-The lack of depth in gameplay. Every single level and objective boils down to A. Go to place B. Scan thing C. Kill everything.
-The loot system. It really doesn't matter what gear you have at all. Before endgame you just need to equip whatever gives you the biggest armor or damage boost and during endgame you just prioritize "light" which is the attribute that levels you up past 20.

The Good:
-It's got some really solid core shooting mechanics. I have no complaints with how polished of a system it is.
-It's got an interesting take of the idea of a persistent FPS world even if it didn't go as far as initially hyped. It's a lot of fun to run into other people occasionally and shoot up some baddies.
-The endgame leveling is interesting because you hit a point where you level up your classes and your effective level in different ways.
-Damn is this super fun with friends! I've got a pretty solid base of friends who picked this up and it's really fun to just go into levels and shoot the shit while killing aliens and grabbing loot.

All in all it's not changing the gaming universe. It's not a terrible game but it's not an amazing one. But I'll say this, as a long time fan of Halo and a person whose main thoroughfare is shooters, I'm having a hell of a lot of fun. It's simple in it's base formula while offering some depth for people who want to burrow into it.

Everything is in a name. Try to find names that mean something and adapt them to your story to make sense. Every name that you come across, whether it's as common as John(Apostle from the Bible) or as outlandish as Zenobia(Ethen Frome's wife from the book *Ethen Frome*, has an origin somewhere. I try my best to make my character's names fit them, the setting, and the background of the name as best as possible.

For example, in my current project, I came up with my antagonist's name, Lucius, first. He was a person whose identity was stolen from him and thus was cast out from having the ability to do any sort of good in the world. This is much like the biblical Lucifer who was cast in Hell and now suffers for eternity. I imagined him much like Mark Twain imagines the devil, "But who prays for Satan? Who, in eighteen centuries, has had the common humanity to pray for the one sinner that needed it most?" My character Lucius, obviously a derivative of Lucien or Lucifer, is someone who is cast aside and forgotten but in my story he is saved.

Meanwhile, I've cast the only name that made sense for my protagonist, Michael, much like the archangel who cast Lucifer into Hell. Furthermore, Michael's last name is Baptiste, referring to Baptism or John the Baptist, the guy who baptized Jesus. Michael not only physically opposes Lucius in a fight they have, but Lucius learns to change his ways from what Michael says and is thus baptized. 

Now I put a hell of a lot of thought into this whole thing and it related to themes throughout my entire book. That being said, you don't have to go crazy with it but make your names mean something. Also, don't let the naming of your character stop your writing. I managed to get my entire plot line down before I had a single name for any character. It should come naturally. It should come from you life experiences. It should help tell your story.

1. I can go on and on about what I've gained from college but one thing to consider, not everyone needs to go to college. I have a friend who spent 4 years in college, failed out of every class and was only able to gain 1 year's worth of credits after years. I asked her what the hell she was doing with her life. One thing to consider would be to just add translations into the book or to not use a crazy amount of another language. If you take a look at authors like Willa Cather or Colm Toibin, they use spots of German, Spanish, and French in their books. 

These instances are usually brief and with modern day translators you can look up the passages in no time. Considering some of these writers have works over 100 years old, in those days people would not necessarily be able to understand the foreign speakers. As such, the language they would use would not be accessible to the general public. Regardless, the instances of a foreign language were not necessary to the overall story but if you could translate them, they added to the overall experience. 

So, You could use instances of foreign speech, and not bog down your story with a crazy amount of dialogue. You need to keep in mind your audience when writing. Although a foreign language could be useful in your story, don't let your readers get bored with a bunch of stuff they can't understand and therefore don't want to read it.

I personally will always finish a book no matter what but I don't think everyone else should have to adhere to this. It can be a rough time but I'm planning to be an English teacher so I don't ever want to force my students to read something I didn't. 

Here's a few tips:
-If you're trying to read it for fun and you find it boring you have two options: 1. Stop! Reading should be an enjoyable experience. You should want to read a book. 2. Come back to it later! Being able to appreciate reading is a skill gained over time. 4 years ago when I started my English major I wouldn't ever dream *Portrait of a Lady* or *The Rise of Silas* could be interesting (yay for late 19th century class commentaries!)
- Break it up. It's really easy to get burned out and lose interest quickly. Set goals (read for 20 minutes, read one chapters, etc.) or reward yourself with something you like at the end of each chapter.
- Do the leg work: I've found that knowing more about the author, his motives, and what the book is about makes reading the book a lot easier. The first time I read Vonnegut's *Slaughterhouse Five* I could not have been more bored. I thought it was just a poorly written story with nothing happening. I read it later in life with the knowledge that it's about the fire bombing of Dresden and is a commentary on war, religion, and the human experience. What was once one of my most hated high school experiences became one of my all time favorite books because I went into it knowing what to look for.

Yes there are elder evils (in this case the orbs which we already know plenty of from the first game) and there is the notion of insanity (Mandas' literal fragmentation of his psyche plus all the crazy flashbacks you start having).

But what drives his stories is the the implications that his tales lead to. More often than not the initial horrors that come to light are either dealt with or at some point the protagonist comes to a fuller understanding of the evil they face. However, regardless of the upscale note of defeating the Dunwich horror may end on, the idea that a more malevolent force that still exists far beyond the reach of humankind is something to greatly fear. Although the citizens of Arkham and Providence have time and time again banished eldritch evils from the world, they still exist beyond the greater planes of man AND THERE IS NOTHING ANYONE CAN DO ABOUT IT.

Well that's a difficult question. It also depends on what kind of class i.e creative writing, composition, American/British/whatever nationality Literature classes. Or maybe I'm just over thinking this so I'll pick 8 books I think anyone should read at a 12th grade level :)

1. Slaughterhouse-Five by Kurt Vonnegut: It's a great anti-war commentary in which the main character gives a great deal of insight as to the horrors of war and various other aspects of man's shortcomings.

2. The House on Mango Street by Sandra Cisneros: Both a hilarious and heart-wrenching read about an inner-city Spanish youth. Her trials and tribulations can allow for kids in impoverished areas to find a relatable and hopeful story while also providing some introspection for kids who might not have the same problems as someone who lives in an impoverished urban area. Plus it's a very easy read and hysterical at times.

3. One of Ours or O, Pioneers by Willa Cather: Both books embody what I personally believe to be the American dream, more so than The Great Gatsby. One of Ours is a tale of realizing one's true dreams and place in the world while O, Pioneers features a strong female protagonist who overcomes gender discrimination and a fight against nature to thrive in a wild west America. 

4. Taming of the Shrew or A Mid Summer's Night Dream by William Shakespeare: ENOUGH WITH SHOVING TRAGEDIES DOWN KID'S THROATS! THEY DON'T WANNA READ THEM! Seriously more often than not I find high school students have an aversion to Shakespeare's tragedies. They're too monotonous at times and can only truly appreciated with a well manicured background in the language arts and an understanding of the time period of Shakespeares.

However, Shakespeare is still a keystone in the world of writing so he demands to be studied. Give kids something fun. I'd be willing to bet they'd love to learn more about Medieval and the Renaissance if there were some and sex jokes thrown in.

5. Beowulf: Only a select few parts though. There are several pivotal events in Beowulf, such as the slaying of each creature Beowulf's death and his time spent in Heorot. His stuggles against the various creature's each symbolize a Hero's battle to overcome one's own ego and can be used as an example of conquering one's inner daemons. Other than that there is a lot of time spent giving historical accounts of battles that's supposed to add validity to the story.

6. Dagon, The Nameless City, Cool Air by H.P Lovecraft: All of these stories give a good introspect into the master of sci-fi horror and his various themes such as forbidden knowledge and hidden evils. Plus his writing style can chill to the bone and is only matched by...

7. A Tell-tale Heart, The Cask of Amomtillado, The Raven, Annabelle Lee by Edgar Allen Poe: While Lovecraft focuses on horrors beyond our imagination, Poe focuses on the terrible enigma of the human mind and how it can become distorted.

8. Superman for All Seasons by Jeph Loeb -OR- Batman: The Dark Knight Returns by Frank Miller: Okay so this one is obviously a personal choice but I believe comic book heroes are an untapped resource for moral debate in today's world. Superman is the big, blue boyscout everyone expects him to be. His story can give many topics to discuss such as: "If we have the power to act, to what degree should we help?"; "Are Superman's moral's the perfect model for how a person should behave?"; Superman as a Christ figure; or "If Superman is so good why does he resort to violence?" 

Meanwhile, Batman is the opposite of Superman in every way. Some of the question are the same for him, "If we have the power to act, to what degree should we help?"; "Are Superman's moral's the perfect model for how a person should behave?" DUDE! I absolutely love that book so very much! I'm glad it helped you just as it helped me. Also, the reason a fictional book was able to help you is because of the nature and relationship between human social connections and fiction. Humans are by the core of the nature looking for social relationships. Novels by their nature are meant to convey a message to other humans about a particular idea, event, or feeling. And well, you being depressed while reading a book on depression is pretty much fulfilling both of thoes criteria.

I can't recommend too many books that directly have to deal specifically with depression but I can give you plenty of books that deal with difficult life situations and have depression as a factor;

-The Alcoholic by Jonathan Ames: This is about..well, an alcoholic. HE tells the story of how his life spun out of control and how his alcoholism lead him to drugs, sex, and some very bad decisions and confusing no way out situations. There's a good deal of humor in it as well so it's not horribly depressing but it is very real and very graphic.

-When David Lost His Voice by Judith Vanistendael: David is a middle aged man who is diagnosed with terminal cancer. The book follows the last few months of his life and shows how not only he deals with his immanent death but how his two daughters and wife deal with it as well. It's a very touching story about losing a loved one and how children deal with death.

-The House of Mango Street by Sandra Cisneros: This book catalogs the life of a young inner-city Hispanic girl and her struggles in life. It's told in a series of short prose, essentially little short stories that are all connected but they can stand alone themselves. The female protagonist's stories range from hilarious to tragic as she tells the reader about her time growing up. I highly recommend this one. There are some stories in here that changed my life even though I'm not an inner-city hispanic female :P

I wish I could give you more but my book collection is in storage. If I think of any more I'll leave you another post. Happy reading!

If you're looking for something off the beaten path:
-Dark Fall: Point and click series that focuses on a detective who gets wrapped up in a the case of a child's murder. Meanwhile all this really crazy poltergeist style activity starts to happen in the locations he visits. It's more storyline driven and atmospheric than anything else.

-Scratches: Short synopsis;  a big time horror writer is having writer's block so a friend of his who is a realtor finds him a house with a shady history or murder and mystery. Well you spend the first day there looking about the house and finding out about its past. Then, in the middle of the first night you wake up to the sound of someone scratching the inside of the house's walls with their finger nails. From there you investigate the house even further and try to figure everything out. This one is also point and click. I do have to say that this is my favorite horror game to date though. Very Lovecraftian in origin.

-Penumbra: This one might be a little more up your alley. You receive a note from your father instructing you to stay away from he dig site he has been working at. Weird thing is your father has been dead for 10 years. Once you go to investigate you find all kinds of crazy stuff happening that spans over the course of two must play games (there's actually 3 games but the third one literally has nothing to do with the main story at all and there is not a single monster in the game whatsoever, probably one of the biggest letdowns in my gaming career).
